title: High availability, scalability, reliability and predictability
learningObjective: Describe high availability, scalability (vertical and horizontal) and elasticity, and explain how the cloud improves reliability and predictability.
foundation: High availability: your service keeps running even when something fails. Azure backs services with SLAs (service level agreements) such as 99.9% or 99.99% uptime.

Scalability: adding resources to handle more load. Scale up (vertical) = a bigger machine. Scale out (horizontal) = more machines. Elasticity is scaling automatically as demand changes, and scaling back down.
Reliability: the ability to recover from failures and keep working. Azure's global regions let you run in more than one place, so one disaster doesn't stop you.
Predictability: you can predict both performance (autoscaling and load balancing keep it steady) and cost (tools forecast and track spending).
engineer: SLA maths: 99.9% allows about 43.8 minutes of downtime a month; 99.99% about 4.4 minutes. When an app depends on several services, the composite SLA is the product: 99.95% × 99.99% ≈ 99.94%, lower than either.
High availability techniques: redundancy (several instances), availability zones (separate datacenters in a region), load balancing, health probes, and automatic failover.
Scale up/down: change VM size or service tier (often a brief restart). Scale out/in: add or remove instances (Virtual Machine Scale Sets, App Service instances); usually no downtime.
Elasticity is driven by autoscale rules (for example 'add an instance when average CPU > 70% for 10 minutes', 'remove when < 30%') or schedules.

Reliability: decentralised design across zones and regions, backups, geo-replication, and disaster recovery (Azure Site Recovery). The Well-Architected Framework reliability pillar gives design guidance.
Performance predictability: autoscale, load balancing and high availability. Cost predictability: pricing calculator, Cost Management forecasts, budgets and analytics.

example.title: A news site on election night
body: Traffic jumps 20× for one night. Autoscale adds web instances as CPU rises (elasticity) and removes them after midnight. Instances span three availability zones behind a load balancer (high availability).
The database is geo-replicated to another region (reliability), and finance set a budget alert with a forecast (predictability).

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources
portal: VM scale set or App Service plan > Scaling: add autoscale rules and instance limits.
VM > Size: scale up or down.
Service level agreements are published per service on the Microsoft licensing site.
configuration.cli:
az monitor autoscale create -g <rg> --resource <vmss-id> --min-count 2 --max-count 10 --count 2
az monitor autoscale rule create -g <rg> --autoscale-name <name> --condition "Percentage CPU > 70 avg 10m" --scale out 1

troubleshooting.symptom: App is slow at peak even with autoscale.
troubleshooting.cause: Maximum instance count reached, or scale rule threshold too high.
troubleshooting.fix: Raise the maximum and lower the threshold; check for a bottleneck in the database.
Scale out with multiple instances instead.

comparisons.difference: Scalability is the ability to grow; elasticity is growing and shrinking automatically.
HA keeps a service up through component failures; DR restores service after a major event such as a region outage.

misconceptions.reality: It defines an uptime commitment and service credits if it's missed.

misconceptions.myth: Scaling up and scaling out are the same.
The cloud is automatically highly available.
misconceptions.reality: You must design for it, for example with zones and multiple instances.

architectureDecisions: Prefer scale-out with autoscale for web tiers.
Deploy across availability zones for higher SLAs.
Calculate the composite SLA of all dependencies.
